concept.name: Moving average crossover
concept.definition: A signal framework in which a shorter-period moving average crossing a longer-period one (or price crossing a moving average) is read as a shift in trend direction; John Murphy calls the two-average version the double crossover method. It is an analytical convention, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: When the fast average overtakes the slow one, recent prices have moved enough to bend the trend measure — a simple, mechanical trend-change rule.
concept.mechanics: Bullish signal: the short MA crosses above the long MA; bearish: short crosses below. Common pairs are 5/35 (short-term) and 50/200 (long-term); a triple-crossover variant uses three averages. MACD(12,26,1) quantifies EMA crossovers as the fast-minus-slow difference.
concept.failure_modes: Both averages lag, so signals are late by construction and whipsaw repeatedly in trendless markets; the documented Home Depot example shows three whipsaws before one successful 20%+ signal.
concept.misconceptions: A crossover describes what has already happened; it does not predict continuation. Unfiltered crossover systems are unreliable — price or time filters are typically needed.
concept.example: A 10-day EMA crossing above a 50-day EMA is a bullish crossover; with MACD(10,50,1), the MACD line crossing zero marks the same event.

citations.source: Moving Averages - Simple and Exponential | ChartSchool | StockCharts.com
